PEPTIDES DU VIRUS VARICELLE-ZONA ET AUTRES VIRUS PERMETTANT D'ASSURER UN DIAGNOSTIC ET UNE THERAPIE DANS LE CAS DU VIH-2

abstract.p: Viral chimeric peptides useful for HIV diagnostic testing and therapy of HIV are described which comprise a loop sequence from a Varicella-Zoster virus protein and additional portion(s) that enhance antigenic reactivity of the loop with anti-HIV antibody. The peptides typically are at least 16 amino acid residues long and advantageously contain additional portions that have some sequence identity with peptide sequences adjacent to a cystine loop of HIV-1 gp41. The peptides immunologically cross-react with protein from a wide variety of HIV-2 strains. Peptides according to some embodiments of the invention are less hydrophobic and more basic for improved water solubility compared to peptides from naturally occurring strains of HIV. These chimeric peptides differ greatly from the naturally occurring sequences and are not identified as corresponding to any particular viral species or strain.

L'invention concerne des peptides chimères utiles à des fins de diagnostic et de thérapie pour le VIH. Ils comprennent une séquence en boucle issue de la protéine du virus varicelle-zona et une ou plusieurs parties additionnelles qui améliorent la réactivité antigénique de la boucle vis-à-vis d'un anticorps anti-VIH. Généralement, les peptides ont une longueur d'au moins 16 acides aminés et, ce qui est avantageux, ils renferment des parties additionnelles qui ont une identité de séquence avec les séquences peptidiques qui sont adjacentes à une boucle de cystine de gp41 du VIH-1. Les peptides en question ont une activité immunologique croisée avec la protéine d'un large éventail de souches du VIH-2. Selon certaines variantes, les peptides considérés sont moins hydrophobes et plus basiques, ce qui permet d'améliorer leur solubilité dans l'eau par rapport aux peptides issus de souches de VIH d'origine naturelle. Lesdits peptides chimères diffèrent largement des séquences d'origine naturelle et ne sont pas identifiés comme correspondant à des espèces ou à des souches virales particulières.

description.p: Peptides from Varicella-Zoster and other Viruses for HTV-2 Diagnosis and Therapy
Field of the Invention

The invention relates to diagnostic tests and antigens used in such tests. More specifically, the invention relates to peptide sequences and sequence modifications of peptides that comprise sequences from the open reading frame protein 51 of Varicella-Zoster and which have utility for the detection of HIV-2 infection.
Background of the Invention

The retrovirus known as Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV, also HTLV-LLI), causes Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (AIDS) in humans (Gallo, et al., Science 224:500 (1984); Sarngadharan, et al. , Science. 224:506 (1984), Popovic, et al. , Science 224:497 (1984). Infection by this virus results in the appearance of antibodies in the blood that react against various molecular parts of the virus, particularly the envelope proteins. The antibody-based binding reaction between antibodies from an infected patient and a viral antigen(s) is used in various methods for detection of HIV infection, such as latex agglutination and ELISA. Of the retroviruses, HIV has received the most attention recently because of the widespread damage caused by this virus. Initially, tests developed for detecting HIV infection contained antigens corresponding to protein of the first discovered strains of this virus, termed "HIV-1" as described, for example, by U.S. patent Nos. 4,708,818; 4,647,773 and 5,135,864. Later tests have used additional antigens that, although cross-reacting with HIV-1 types of this virus, generally react more specifically with a later discovered type of HTV termed "HTV-2" as described, for
example, by U.S. patent Nos. 5,055,391; 4,839,288 and 5,066,782. The discovery of yet further strains of this virus species, such as those termed "HIV-3" or "HIV-1 Group O" has prompted the use of additional antigens for detecting HIV infection that react preferably with these samples as described, for example, by U.S. patent Nos. 5,567,603 and 5,304,466. When used in screening for prior HIV exposure, a blood sample typically is contacted with test antigen(s), followed by detection of binding between test antigen and sample antibody. Such detection is complicated not only by the classification of HTV into various strains such as HIV-1, HIV-2, HIV-3 and their various "clades," based on antibody reactivity, but also by the rapid mutation of HTV, even within the same infected individual. A central challenge of HIV testing and therapy is in finding antigens that cross react with these different antigenic types.

One solution to the diversity problem in the diagnostic area has been to include multiple protein antigens in a diagnostic test. In this way separate antigens, each having multiple epitopes from diverse regions of HIV protein can, as a mixture, react with diverse sera of patients infected with HIV. Drawbacks of this strategy include, among other tilings, a higher degree of non-specific binding reactions due to the variety of proteins used and a limitation in the amount of total antigen that can be added to a test, which typically has a small solid phase surface or reaction volume

The HIV antigen diversity problem is a major challenge to successful HIV diagnosis and therapy, and directly causes false test results. Unpublished co-pending applications 60/091,659 filed July 2, 1998 (attorney docket No. 073294/0160), 60/072,863 filed January 28, 1998 (attorney docket No. 073294/0161), 60/072,981 filed January 29, 1998 (attorney docket No. 073294/0162), 60/088,229 filed June 5, 1998 (attorney docket No. 073294/0172), 60/100,422 filed September 15, 1998 (attorney docket No. 073294/0191), 60/112,026 filed December 11, 1998 (attorney docket No. 073294/0178), 60/(1104,686) filed October 16, 1998 (attorney docket No. 073294/0197) and 60/104,685 filed October 16, 1998 (attorney docket No. 073294/0198), which are herein incorporated in their entireties by reference, teach how to engineer "Universal" peptides that react more broadly with various strains of HIV to address this problem. Those applications also describe an approach that replaces a large recombinant protein having many different epitopes from various regions of HTV with one or more peptides that correspond to a single epitopic region of HIV. In this approach, alternate peptides from a common region are engineered to approximate various
epitopes that HIV may differentiate into. This strategy of employing diversity within one immunologically important point of an HIV protein, in contrast to combining diversity between epitopes from various regions, yields improved assays and therapy, as detailed in the above-referenced unpublished applications. For example, U.S. No. 60/104,685 describes an SP and HIV-1 chimera that simulates a primordial HIV protein epitope sequence that cross- reacts with a surprisingly broad range of HIV strains.

Because of the close genetic relationship between HIV-1 and HIV-2 strains, antigens that resemble HIV-1 protein epitope(s) may react with antibodies made from exposure to HTV-2 strains. Conversely, antigens designed from lysates, proteins and peptides from HTV- 2 may cross-react with HIV-1 strains. Accordingly, there is a need for antigens that react more specifically with HIV-2 strains in order to classify an infection as originating from an HIV-1 strain or an HIV-2 strain.

The sensitivity of HIV detection is another important problem in HIV detection that is influenced by the test antigen used. If a test could be made more sensitive by use of a more reactive antigen, the test could detect HIV detection at an earlier time, and thus allow earlier treatment. Thus, there is a continuing need for HIV antigens that react more strongly with antibodies in test samples.

Of course, there is an urgent need for antigens that are potent for HIV therapy as well as for HIV detection. The rapid mutation of HIV allows the virus a quick genetic response to escape destruction by the immune system. Thus, new HIV antigens, particularly antigens modeled after broader features that are not limited to a specific type of virus and that display new epitopes can directly be used for therapy and prophylaxis against HIV infection as well.
Summary of the Invention

It is an object of the invention to improve the test specificity of HIV detection by providing a peptide sequence that reacts well with sera from patients infected with HTV-2 strains and that reacts less well with sera from patients infected with HIV-1 strains. It is another object of the invention to provide peptide sequences that improve HTV-2 test sensitivity over existing tests using previously known antigens. It is yet another object of the invention to provide peptide vaccines against infectious agents. It is another object of the
invention to provide methods for deriving HIV-2 antigen cross-reactive peptides and methods for testing HIV-2 infection. Further objects of the invention readily will be apparent from the disclosure herein.

One embodiment of the invention is a peptide useful for detecting HTV-2 infection, preferably having a length of at least 16 amino acid residues, and comprising a core Varicella-Zoster protein 51 sequence of SEQ ID NO: 1 (C-A-F-R-Q-Xl-C) wherein XI is selected from the group consisting of R, I, L. V. T, H, Q, C, W, F, and Y.

Another embodiment of the invention is a peptide useful for detecting HTV-2 infection, having a length of at least 16 amino acid residues, and comprising a core sequence A-W-G-C-A-F-R-Q combined with a sequence from the immunodominant region of gp41 from HIV-1.

Another embodiment of the invention is a method for improving a peptide useful for HTV-2 testing, comprising replacing a hydrophobic amino acid of the peptide with a less hydrophobic amino acid. Yet another embodiment of the invention is a method for improving a peptide useful for HIV-2 testing, comprising increasing the alpha helix content of the peptide. In yet another embodiment, the increase in alpha helix content is made outside of a cystine loop immunodominant region.

Another embodiment of the invention is a reagent for immunological detection of anti- HTV antibody in a blood sample, comprising a dried antigen that, upon rewetting with water or a clinical sample, substantially reacts with antibodies from patients exposed to HTV-2, wherein said antigen is between 16-50 amino acids long and possesses a sequence described herein. Another embodiment is a method of detecting HTV-2 infection, comprising incubating a blood sample or blood derivative with a peptide described herein, followed by determination of binding between antibody in the blood sample or blood derivative and the peptide. Yet another embodiment is a kit for determining infection with HTV-2, comprising instructions for how to use (for example, an instruction booklet, label or electronic message) and a device for detecting the presence of anti-HIV-2 antibody in a blood sample or blood derivative, wherein the device comprises a peptide described herein.

Yet another embodiment of the invention is a method of improving reactivity of an antigenic peptide for a diagnostic test of HIV. comprising replacing a seven amino acid long cystine loop segment of the HIV-1 gp41 protein or the HIV-2 gp36 protein with a sequence selected from the group consisting of SEQ ID NO: 3 CAFRQRC; SEQ ID NO: 19
CAFRQIC; SEQ ID NO: 20 CAFRQQC; SEQ ID NO: 21 CAFRQTC; SEQ ID NO: 22 CAFRQCC; SEQ ID NO: 23 CAFRQLC; SEQ ID NO: 24 CAFRQWC; SEQ ID NO: 25 CAFRQHC; SEQ ID NO: 26 CAFRQFC and SEQ ID NO: 27 CAFRQYC.

Yet another embodiment of the invention is a method of increasing HTV-2 cross- reactivity of an antigenic peptide for a diagnostic test of HIV. comprising replacing a seven amino acid long cystine loop segment of the HIV-1 gp41 protein with a sequence selected from the group consisting of SEQ ID NO: 99 C-A-G-R-Q-V-C: SEQ ID NO: 100 C-A-G-K- Q-V-C; SEQ ID NO: 101 C-A-G-R-L-V-C; SEQ ID NO: 102 C-A-D-R-Q-V-C; SEQ ID NO: 103 C-A-N-R-Q-V-C; and SEQ ID NO: 104 C-A-G-K-L-V-C. Another embodiment of the invention is a method of improving reactivity of an antigenic peptide for a diagnostic test of HTV-2, comprising replacing a leucine ("L"), isoleucine ("I") or valine ("V") from the peptide with a hydrophilic amino acid.

A further embodiment is a method of detecting HIV-2 infection from a blood sample with a whole blood assay device, the device comprising a blood filter that contacts a reagent layer that contains at least one peptide described herein, wherein the method comprises applying one or more drops of whole blood to the blood filter and determining the presence of one or more visual reactions in response to the presence of anti-HIV antibody in the blood sample.

Detailed Description of the Preferred Embodiments

The inventors have explored chimeric peptides from various viruses and virus strains for the purpose of improving the sensitivity and selectivity of HIV tests and therapeutics. This work led to several discoveries relating to chimeric peptides formed from a Varicella- Zoster protein and peptide sequences of HIV-1 protein, which provide unexpected improvements in HIV testing and therapy, particularly for HIV-2 testing. This work also led to a discovery of broadly reactive peptide sequences that contain epitopes which represent epitopes of an evolutionary precursor of primate immunodeficiency virus. Peptides according to this embodiment cross-react with a variety of strains that infect human that are classified as
HTV-1, HTV-1 Group O and HIV-2 These discoveries are discussed separately below, together with related embodiments of the invention
Varicella-zoster - HTV-1 Chimeric Peptides with Superior Properties for Detecting HTV
(1) Combine a V. zoster Gene 51 cystine loop with an HIV-1 Antigen-loop Enhancer

The inventors explored cystine loop regions of viral proteins and selected a Vancella- zoster ("Varicella-Zoster") virus gene 51 product sequence C-A-F-R-Q-R-C sequence (SEQ ID NO 3) for further study This 7 ammo acid sequence differs from a cystme loop sequence C-A-F-R-Q-V-C (SEQ ID NO 4) common to both simian and human viruses by a hydrophobic (V) to basic (R) amino acid substitution Chimeric peptides comprised of the seven residue Varicella-Zoster sequence and of HIV-1 peptide sequences were prepared and studied for use in HIV detection Peptide chimeras that comprised, along with the Varicella- Zoster sequence, increasing length of HIV-1 peptide showed correspondingly increased reactivity in HTV lmmunoassays, particularly HIV-2 assays

The term "chimera as used here, means that the peptide is a composite of peptide sequences that come from two different species or types of viruses, for example the HTV-1 species of virus and the Varicella-Zoster species of virus In some advantageous embodiments, however, the portion from the HIV-1 species of virus differs significantly and is not identifiable as belonging to any particular strain or species Furthermore, the portion from the Varicella-Zoster species can be modified according to certain principles enumerated herein or otherwise apparent to the skilled person, and after modification is not identifiable as belongmg to any particular virus strain or species

A chimera according to an embodiment of the invention, comprises a 7 ammo acid Varicella-Zoster segment and at least 9, preferably at least 11 and more advantageously at least 15 or more ammo acid residues attached to at least one end of the Varicella-Zoster segment The Varicella-Zoster protein 51 sequence is taught by Davidson and Scott, /. Gen. Virol 67 1759-1816 (1986)

In an embodiment of the invention, the added ammo acids form a sequence that antigemcally enhances a known HTV-1 gp41 immunodominant region sequence The term "antigenically enhances a known HTV-1 gp41 immunodominant region sequence" means an antigen that comprises a sequence which, when combined with a 7 member cystme loop
sequence from an HTV-1 strain (for ex. C-K-G-K-L-I-C) enhances that sequence's cross- reactivity with antibodies specific for a known naturally occurring gp41 sequence. Furthermore, an enhancing peptide sequence as termed here, typically shares at least some sequence identity with a corresponding known sequence that is adjacent (contiguous to) the cystine loop of this protein. By way of example, SEQ ID NO: 5 (L-E-D-Q-A-R-L-N-A-W- G-C-A-F-R-Q-R-C) shares 64% sequence homology with the Group O subtype M consensus sequence of SEQ ID NO: 105 (L-K-D-Q-Q-L-L-N-L-W-G-C-K-G-K-L-I-C) because 7 of the 11 amino acids outside the loop have the same identity. In making this comparison, only amino acids within 25 positions of the loop should be considered. In an advantageous embodiment, the amino acids within 25 positions from the loop share less than 70% sequence homology with a known HIV-1 env41 protein.

The identity comparison used to select a suitable sequence to link with the Varicella Zoster cystine loop segment is founded on the inventors' discovery that amino acids positioned near (i.e. within about 25 amino acids, particularly within 21 amino acids) the cystine loop affect the antigenicity of the loop and often have no cross-reactivity with anti- HTV-1 antibodies in the absence of the cystine loop. Generally, the neighboring amino acid residues which affect the loop antigenicity contain at least 30% and more advantageously, at least 50% sequence identity with a corresponding known gp41 protein sequence. When making this comparison, it is advantageous to look at the segment of amino acids adjacent to the amino terminal side of the loop. In another embodiment, however, residues on both the amino terminal side and the carboxyl terminal side of the loop are considered.

A large number of "antigenically enhancing" sequences work according to this formula. Co-pending U.S. patent applications 60/091,659 filed July 2, 1998 (attorney docket No. 073294/0160), 60/072,863 filed January 28, 1998 (attorney docket No. 073294/0161), 60/072,981 filed January 29, 1998 (attorney docket No. 073294/0162), 60/098,705 filed September 1, 1998 (attorney docket No. 073294/0168), 60/088,229 filed June 5, 1998 (attorney docket No. 073294/0172), 60/100,422 filed September 15, 1998 (attorney docket No. 073294/0191), 60/(104,686) filed October 16, 1998 (attorney docket No. 073294/0197), PCT application "Universal Peptides" filed June 4, 1999 (attorney docket No. 036034/0106) and 60/104,685 filed October 16, 1998 (attorney docket No. 073294/0198) describe antigenically enhancing sequences according to the meaning used herein. A peptide comprising at least a 7 amino acid long segment of a sequence listed in one of these
referenced applications can be combined with a Varicella Zoster loop to form a chimera. This sequence is continuous with the immunodominant loop of gp41, as exemplified by the sequences shown in Figure 1. Each 7 amino acid long or larger sequence from the sequences disclosed in the co-pending applications specifically is contemplated for combining with a Varicella Zoster loop to form a suitable chimera according to the invention. Within the chimera, the HIV-1 enhancing peptide portion facilitates reaction of the cystine loop portion from Varicella Zoster with antibodies from at least some HIV-2 infected blood samples. Preferably, such chimeric peptides cross-react with a large variety of HIV-2 infected samples. Even more preferably, such chimeras do not react well with HIV-1 samples and are useful to distinguish between HTV-1 and HIV-2 infection.

In another embodiment, the amino acid sequence(s) added to the Varicella-Zoster sequence are known sequences from HTV-1. particularly HIV-1 Group O, as described by, for example, by Eberle et al. J. Vir. Meth. 67: 85,88 (1997) and U.S. Nos. 5,567,603 and 5,304,466. According to yet further embodiments, a naturally occurring sequence is further modified as described in one or more of the co-pending applications referred to above.

Chimeras in accordance with the invention may include an antigenically enhancing HTV-1 sequence on the amino terminal side of the Varicella-Zoster loop and/or an antigenically enhancing HIV-1 sequence on the carboxyl terminal side of the Varicella-Zoster loop. Most advantageously, the chimera comprises an enhancing sequence portion of at least 11 amino acids long on the amino terminal side and contiguous with the loop.

It is emphasized that the claimed peptides and peptides constructed according to principles of the invention differ significantly from naturally occurring forms and are not identified as belonging to any particular viral species or strain. Furthermore, these chimeras were found to have new and advantageous properties for HIV tests, and particularly for tests of infection by HIV-2.
(2) Preferred Helix Turn Profile for the Di-cysteine Loop Region of the Chimera

The cystine loop sequence taken from the Varicella-Zoster protein may be modified according to certain principles. Derivatives of the cystine sequence of Varicella-Zoster ORF 51 protein which evince a "s-s-s-s-h-s-s" helix turn profile, when modeled by the peptide analysis software program, "Peptide Companion Version 1.24 for Windows" from Peptides

International, Inc. Louisville, Kentucky 40299 U.S.A. are particularly useful. As revealed
by output from this program, the Varicella-Zoster cystine loop structure differs conformationally from the HIV-1 gp41 immunodominant region loop, which lacks a helix twist.

The inventors discovered that the different conformation of the Varicella-Zoster loop is advantageous for engineering peptides for HTV tests and therapy. Furthermore, changes to this loop sequence which maintain the s-s-s-s-h-s-s mrn profile, as determined by use of the referenced software, are useful for peptides in accordance with further embodiments of the invention. For example, the following sequences have the advantageous peptide mrn profile and represent further embodiments: SEQ ID NO: 19 CAFRQIC; SEQ ID NO: 20 CAFRQQC; SEQ ID NO: 21 CAFRQTC; SEQ ID NO: 22 CAFRQCC; SEQ ID NO: 23 CAFRQLC; SEQ ID NO: 24 CAFRQWC; SEQ ID NO: 25 CAFRQHC; SEQ ID NO: 26 CAFRQFC and SEQ ID NO: 27 CAFRQYC. According to an embodiment of the invention, a chimeric peptide advantageously comprises a Varicella-Zoster sequence chosen from this list linked with one or more peptide sequences that antigenically enhance the HTV-1 loop. The namral Varicella-Zoster sequence of CAFRQRC, however, is preferred because peptides having this sequence give superior performance under some conditions. For example, replacing the arginine in this sequence with isoleucine caused greater non-specific background when used in an immunoassay. as seen by the data of Figure 3. and the naturally occurring arginine is advantageous at this position.

(3) Decrease Bulk Hydrophobicity within the Varicella-Zoster Loop Sequence Another discovery from the study of Varicella Zoster protein sequences was that peptides having a lower bulk hydrophobicity within the cystine loop region cross-react more specifically with HIV-2 antigens. Figure 5 depicts the hydrophobicity scale of a representative (HTV/SIV) primate gp36 immunodominant loop sequence (SEQ ID NO. 16) and of a more hydrophilic (less hydrophobic) sequence of Varicella Zoster (SEQ ID NO. 17) according to this embodiment of the invention. Figure 6 shows, for example, a comparison profile of another sequence in accordance with the invention (SEQ ID NO. 18) with the primate loop sequence SEQ ID NO. 16. These figures show predicted bulk hydrophobicity of sequences obtained with the software cited above.

Most advantageous embodiments of the invention according to this discovery are peptides comprising a cystine loop region that comprises an arginine adjacent to the amino
terminal side of the loop amino terminal cysteine residue, as shown by, for example, SEQ ID NO. 3. Without wishing to be bound by a particular theory of this embodiment of their invention, the inventors theorize that the antigenically active cysteine loop portion of a peptide in accordance with the embodiment is solvated better and reacts better with components of the immune system by virtue of its better water solubility. Furthermore, this feature is particularly important when the peptide is attached to a particle or other solid phase such as a membrane used in diagnostic tests. Keeping the cystine loop off the solid phase surface helps the loop react faithfully with antibodies and other components of the immune system. The claimed peptides described herein, in fact, are particularly useful for solid phase binding assays wherein a peptide is immobilized onto a solid phase. Thus, having an arginine, or other amino acid that is less hydrophilic than valine, in the 6th position of this loop provides an advantageous peptide, particularly when the amino acid is chosen to maintain a predicted s-s-s-s-h-s-s helix mm profile, and also particularly when it is desired to keep the loop in solution with the non-loop portion attached, directly, or indirectly via a conjugated moiety, to a solid phase.
(4) Increase Bulk Hydrophobicity in the Region Adjacent to the Amino Terminal Side of the Varicella-Zoster Loop Sequence

Yet another discovery from a study of the Varicella-Zoster sequence is that increasing the bulk hydrophobicity character of the peptide portion adjacent to the amino terminal side of the cystine loop portion yields a peptide antigen with improved characteristics such as sensitivity or selectivity in HIV-2 infection tests. Figure 5 depicts a comparison between this portion of the HIV-2/SIV primate sequence and the Varicella-Zoster sequence. The Varicella Zoster sequence is significantly more hydrophobic than the HIV-2 sequence in this region. Figure 6 compares this portion of primate sequence with the corresponding portion of a chimeric peptide in accordance with the invention.

Without wishing to be bound by any particular theory of this embodiment of the invention, the inventors theorize that the increased hydrophobic character of the portion adjacent to the amino terminal side of the loop helps stabilize the alpha helix there because that portion forms less hydrogen bonding and ionic binding with water and other molecules, which could interfere with its structure. Furthermore, the hydrophobic character helps orient the cysteine loop region into the aqueous medium by binding to a solid surface when used in
immunoassays. In one embodiment, a more hydrophobic portion from 1 to 6 amino acids off of the amino terminal side of the cystine is particularly advantageous when the peptide is used as an immobilized binding partner in an immunoassay. In this use, the more hydrophobic region is at least 6 amino acids long, and is "more hydrophobic" than the corresponding portion of a naturally occurring peptide sequence such as the HIV-2/STV sequence exemplified in Figure 5 and as determined by prediction of bulk hydrophobicity with the above-referenced software program.

Each chimeric peptide according to an embodiment of the invention is useful for detecting HIV infection. That is, each chimera has the biochemical quality of binding at least some antibody from at least one sample of HIV infected blood. Most advantageously, in this respect is the quality of antibody binding to peptides. Thus, each chimera according to this embodiment can be used in an HIV test that reacts with at least one HIV-2 infectious sample to yield a positive test result. Binding assays used for this purpose are well known, and can be carried out by various procedures, such as an ELISA test or dot-blot assay described herein.
(5) Increase Secondary Structure of the Chimeric Peptide

It was further discovered that increasing the amount of secondary structure of the chimeric peptide, particularly outside the cystine loop region provides improved HTV-2 detection. Secondary structure in this context refers to polypeptide helix or pleated sheet that forms primarily by multiple hydrogen bonding between peptide bond hydrogen and oxygen. Most advantageous is alpha helix strucmre that forms within a stretch of the peptide to the amino teπninal side of the loop.

The inventors discovered that placing or increasing alpha helix on the amino terminal side of the cystine loop Varicella-Zoster portion in particular stabilizes the antigen structure. The degree of stabilization has a great influence on performance of a peptide used in diagnosis or therapy. For example, the inventors discovered that adding a five amino acid long helix portion "A-W-E-K-T" to the amino terminal end of an 18 mer chimera comprised of a Varicella-Zoster sequence with an antigenically enhancing HIV-1 sequence provided greater test sensitivity. These data are shown in Figures 2 and 3.

Without wishing to be bound by any one theory of an embodiment of the invention, the inventors theorize that adding this 5 amino acid long helix, which is not a known epitope
of HTV, increases structural stability of the peptide when used in an aqueous environment for binding reactions with anti-HIV-2 antibodies. The increased stability allows the peptide to react more favorably to give more sensitive tests but also changes the immunological characteristics of the antigen. In particular, placement of a tryptophan ("W") at this position 15 residues from the amino terminal side of the cystine loop, decreases cross-reactivity with HTV-1 while maintaining the tendency of this portion of the peptide to form alpha helix and is a particularly advantageous embodiment. The theory of increased stability derives further support from the experimental observation that when this same peptide helix was lengthened by an additional 5 amino acids (to 10 amino acids at the amino terminal portion), the antigen thus formed showed yet even better sensitivity for testing HIV-2. These data are shown in Figure 2. In alternative embodiments, the alpha helix portion may be 6. 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12 or more amino acids long. In other advantageous embodiments alpha helix is added to the carboxyl terminal side of the Varicella-Zoster loop.

Of course, other amino acid combinations, for example, that provide alpha helix extending further away from the amino terminal side of the HIV-1 cystine loop region are advantageous and are contemplated. Biologically functional universal peptides can be prepared through specific mutagenesis of the underlying DNA. The technique further provides a ready ability to prepare and test sequence variants, for example, incorporating one or more of the foregoing considerations, by introducing one or more nucleotide sequence changes into the DNA. Site-specific mutagenesis allows the production of mutants through the use of specific oligonucleotide sequences which encode the DNA sequence of the desired mutation, as well as a sufficient number of adjacent nucleotides, to provide a primer sequence of sufficient size and sequence complexity to form a stable duplex on both sides of the deletion junction being traversed. Typically, a primer of about 17 to 25 nucleotides in length is preferred, with about 5 to 10 residues on both sides of the junction of the sequence being altered. The technique of site-specific mutagenesis is well known in the art, as exemplified by various publications. As will be appreciated, the technique typically employs a phage vector which exists in both a single stranded and double stranded form. Typical vectors useful in site-directed mutagenesis include vectors such as the M13 phage. These phage are readily commercially available and their use is generally well known to those skilled in the art. Double stranded plasmids are also routinely employed in site directed mutagenesis which eliminates the step of transferring the gene of interest from a plasmid to a phage.

Site-directed mutagenesis in accordance herewith is performed by first obtaining a single-stranded vector or melting apart of two strands of a double stranded vector which includes within its sequence a DNA sequence which encodes the desired peptide. An oligonucleotide primer bearing the desired mutated sequence is prepared, generally synthetically. This primer is then annealed with the single-stranded vector, and subjected to DNA polymerizing enzymes such as E. coli polymerase I Klenow fragment, in order to complete the synthesis of the mutation-bearing strand. Thus, a heteroduplex is formed wherein one strand encodes the original non-mutated sequence and the second strand bears the desired mutation. This heteroduplex vector is then used to transform appropriate cells, such as E. coli cells, and clones are selected which include recombinant vectors bearing the mutated sequence arrangement.
The preparation of sequence variants of the selected peptide-encoding DNA segments using site-directed mutagenesis is provided as a means of producing potentially useful species and is not meant to be limiting as there are other ways in which sequence variants of peptides and the DNA sequences encoding them may be obtained. For example, recombinant vectors encoding the desired peptide sequence may be treated with mutagenic agents, such as hydroxylamine, to obtain sequence variants.
Use of the Peptides in Test Devices

Antigens of the instant invention can be used in a wide variety of diagnostic tests that employ antigen-antibody binding for detection of a disease agent. The peptides are particularly useful in dot blot immunoassays such as. for example, described in co-pending application U.S. App. Ser. No. 09/069,935 "Multiple Readout Immunoassay with Improved Resistance to Interferences" (Attorney Docket No. 073294/0173 filed April 30, 1998, incorporated herein in its entirety by reference) and in ELISA assays. The dot-blot immunoassay described in the 09/069,935 application is especially advantageous for detecting HIV infection using a peptide chimera as herein described. This assay uses a test device which has a housing comprised of a water impermeable material which holds other test components such as an absorbent pad with a reagent layer, filter and a reagent used to obtain a test result. The housing has an opening to admit a fluid sample. The housing comes apart during use so that the user can remove the filter to expose the reagent layer for application of a reagent and/or wash fluid. A sleeve that holds the filter is removably attached to the housing such that contact of the filter is favored over contact of the sleeve with the surface of the reagent layer. The sleeve is attached to the housing by a bayonet mount. After a sample is applied, and an optional wash solution added, the sleeve is removed and further optional reagent solution and a wash solution are added directly to the reagent layer. In some applications a sample is added to the device and further processing is carried out at a separate location or after storage of the device for a few hours. In these situations, the sleeve remains attached to the housing to prevent or delay the release of moisture from the device until the later processing steps are carried out. The housing also may contain a cover to protect the opening and further guard against the release of moisture. Acceptable materials for the device housing include water impermeable plastics such as polystyrene, polypropylene, poly vinyl chloride and the like. Acceptable materials for the
filtering portion of the filter, the dispersing portion of the filter, the reagent layer and the absorbent pad are glass fiber, ethyl cellulose, nitrocellulose and ethyl cellulose respectively. When nitrocellulose is used for the reagent layer, however, the material of the filter should be chosen for its ability to premix the test sample and any test reagent that may be present in the filter. Two or more materials can be physically combined to make up a filter, reagent layer or absorbent pad. Two materials are acceptable for the filter, an upper filtering material and a lower dispersal material. Most acceptable is a dispersal layer that passes fluid at a slower flow rate compared to passage of fluid through an upper filtering material. The applicants have found that the use of a dispersal layer is surprisingly superior over the use of a single part filter. Although applicants wish not to be bound by one particular theory of how their dispersal layer works in the assay device, the layer may remove irregularities in the flow that arise from irregular collection of particles in the upper regions of the filter. A second advantage of using a two-part filter is that the dispersal layer, by virtue of its slow fluid flow rate, can prolong one or more reaction times for substances that react before entering the reaction layer, thereby increasing sensitivity.

Advantageously, the dispersal layer extends beyond the sleeve that holds the filter such that when the filter is attached to the container, the dispersal layer portion exerts a greater pressure onto the reagent layer than does the sleeve. "Greater pressure" in this context means that the mechanical force per unit area exerted by the filter onto the reagent layer exceeds the mechanical force per unit area exerted by the sleeve onto the reagent layer. Preferably, the filter exerts at least twice as much mechanical pressure onto the reagent layer compared to the sleeve. More preferably, the sleeve does not contact the reagent layer. By relying principally on the filter itself to contact the reagent layer, the sleeve does not deform the reagent layer. This allows a more even and reproducible transfer of fluid from the filter to the reagent layer. Further advantageous feamres of a test device are found in co-pending application No. 08/933,943 filed on September 19, 1997.

An antigen is immobilized onto the reagent layer portion of the absorbent pad by absorption, via spotting a water solution of the antigen. The optimum amount of antigen to use is determined by methods accepted in the art. The inventors used approximately 150 ng of antigen per test. Chemically synthesized antigens and recombinant antigens can be immobilized within these and other devices by routine methods, such as by spotting a water solution of the antigen onto a nitrocellulose membrane or membrane layer.

After blocking, each well was washed 5 times and blotted. Ten microliters of a sample and 90μl of diluent (2% non-fat milk in phosphate buffered saline with 0.5% NaCI) were added to each well, the well sealed with plastic, and incubated at 37°C for 30 minutes.
